# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up is the most direct test so far of the questions left open by the earlier documents. It uses randomised comparison, record-based output, a stricter hours measure, two-year follow-up, and a pre-registered mediation analysis. Its headline holds up: the per-hour gain in case-processing work shrank but stayed above zero. It also resolves the dispute over the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim. However, the decline is overstated in the summary, the mediation analysis is presented with more certainty than 14 offices can support, and a change in two control offices (which cut their own meetings mid-trial) affects the trial's own estimates.

## Arithmetic check

- **Output per hour at 24 months:**
  - Timesheets: 0.966/0.88 = **+9.8%** ✓
  - System logs: 0.966/0.89 = **+8.5%** ✓
- **Meetings:** treated offices went from 7.4 to 3.9 hours, control offices from 7.2 to 7.0. The relative change is −3.3 hours, consistent with the month-six gap of 3.3 hours. ✓
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100. ✓
- **Halden subset:** 34.9/40.3 = 0.866, so hours fell 13.4%, and 96.8/86.6 = **+11.8%**. ✓

Three figures don't fit together:

1. **Control-office meeting time.** Two control offices cut meetings from 7.1 to 5.0 hours. That alone lowers the average across seven control offices by about 0.6 hours. Yet the reported average change is only −0.2. So the other five control offices must have increased their meeting time by about 0.55 hours each, or the figures don't match. This needs checking.
2. **Counter-office cost.** Adding 12% more staff to offices producing 88.6% of control output gives about 99% of control output for 12% more labour cost. That is roughly **+13% cost per contact** if only labour is counted. The reported 9% only works if non-labour costs are included, or if the extra staff would be more productive. The basis should be stated.
3. **Halden baseline hours.** 40.3 is the baseline for Varga and Holm's 27 organisations with time tracking. The 11 organisations here should be compared with their own baseline. If 40.3 is a shortcut, the 11.8% may be off.

## Main issues

**1. The summary overstates the decline by comparing different hours measures.**
"Fell from 12.5% to 8.5%" compares the 9-month timesheet figure with the 24-month system-log figure. Comparing timesheets at both time points, the decline is 12.5% → 9.8%, about a fifth, and the body text says so. The summary should use that comparison. The confidence intervals at 9 and 24 months overlap widely, so even the decline that is reported is "consistent with" fading, as the authors put it, rather than demonstrated.

**2. The control offices that cut their own meetings affect the main estimate.**
Two of the seven control offices cut meetings at month 15 and gained about 4.1% in output per hour. If that gain lasted, the control group improved by roughly 1 percentage point. That shrinks the treated-versus-control difference by about the same amount. So part of the apparent decline from 9.8% may come from controls improving, not from the treatment effect fading. The report treats the audit only as a side observation. It should also run a sensitivity analysis, either excluding those two offices or adjusting for the audit.

That same observation also offers an important clue. If cutting meetings alone gives a gain of about 4%, a reduced-hours policy may be partly an expensive way to get a cheap reorganisation. The authors say this carefully. It deserves a randomised test of its own.

**3. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.**
- **Too few offices.** The independent units are still 14 offices, so a "larger sample of office-months" does not add independent information. With a total effect of 8.5% (CI 3.4% to 13.8%), the share explained by meetings should be very uncertain. An interval of 28% to 66% looks too narrow and probably reflects office-months being treated as independent. The method for that interval needs to be stated.
- **Mediators were not randomised.** Cutting meetings and improving output could both result from managers being more engaged. The limitations section acknowledges this, but the summary still says "confirms."
- **Measurement error favours meetings.** Meeting time comes from calendars and is measured precisely. Fatigue comes from a questionnaire and is measured with more noise. Noisier measures understate their share, so the 47% versus 18% comparison is probably tilted towards meetings.
- **The data overlap with the data that suggested the idea.** The registration came at month 11, after the 9-month results. If the 24-month model uses office-months from the first year, some of the data overlap with the data that generated the hypothesis.

"Supported by a registered test" is fair. "Confirms" is not.

**4. Where did the baseline meeting data come from?**
The 9-month report said meeting data were collected only in month six, and I noted that this meant no actual cut had been measured. This report gives a baseline of 7.4 hours. It may come from historical calendar records, which would be legitimate, but the source should be stated. This matters because the earlier "cut" claim depended on the same missing baseline.

**5. One of the three Halden reversions does not fit the "coverage" explanation.**
The summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." The marketing agency cited client deadlines. That is deadline-driven work, which the meta-analysis classes as discretionary. It shows that discretionary work can fail too. That point should be stated rather than absorbed into the coverage story.

**6. Questions from the earlier reports are still unanswered.**
- **Case-processing quality and backlog.** The appeal overturn rate is the only quality measure. The 9-month report itself raised the risk of backlogs and missed statutory deadlines. Backlog size, the mix of cases, and deadline breaches are still not reported.
- **Overtime cost.** Output per employee is −3.4% at full pay, and some overtime is claimed. So cost per case rose by at least about 3.5%. The county's own counter-office calculation shows it cares about cost, so the same figure should be given for case-processing.

**7. The Halden attrition problem is not addressed.**
A Halden author co-wrote this report. Varga and Holm showed that the working paper misdescribed when and why nine organisations withdrew. This report makes no mention of it. Also, 9 of the 23 contacted organisations didn't respond. The authors rightly call the respondents "survivors twice over." Given that, "upper bound" is reasonable as an informal description, though not as a strict statistical bound.

## Smaller points

- **Sick days and resignations** are still raw comparisons without confidence intervals.
- **The rebuttals of the earlier papers are fair.**
  - On Varga and Holm: this trial meets the evaluation standards they recommended and still finds a gain.
  - On the meta-analysis: the four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which is exactly the problem I raised. That makes the "no decay" claim unsupported.
- **The month-ten date** attributed to the Halden energy extrapolation was itself miscalculated. A straight-line extrapolation gives about month 8.7. This is minor.

## Where the evidence now stands

- **Well supported:**
  - In discretionary public-sector work, output per actual hour rises by about **8–10%**, and that gain lasts at least two years, possibly somewhat reduced from early levels.
  - Output per employee falls slightly, by about 3%, with the interval including zero.
  - In coverage-bound work, the scheme failed: longer waits, ended at month 12.
- **Moderately supported:**
  - A substantial part of the gain comes from cutting meetings and other low-value time, not from rest alone.
  - Some of that gain may be available without cutting hours.
- **Open:**
  - Whether reorganisation without shorter hours gets most of the gain. Only a trial that compares reorganisation alone with shorter hours, for example a three-arm trial, can answer this.
  - Results beyond two years, in the private sector, and in manufacturing.
  - The full cost per unit of output, including overtime and quality.

I can draft a referee report on this follow-up, or turn the five documents into a one-page evidence brief with the current best estimates and their caveats.
